title: Work with time series
goal: Distinguish calendar dates, observed records, windows, and changes over time.
prerequisites: Parse dates and understand missing values and sorting.

cells.title: Expose a missing day
cells.explanation: A DatetimeIndex lets pandas work with calendar dates. asfreq("D") requests a daily index between the first and last observations. The missing October 4 row appears as unknown, not zero.
cells.code:
df = attendance()
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
result = df.set_index("Date")["Visitors"].sort_index().asfreq("D")
print(result)

questions.answer: One index label per calendar day.

questions.prompt: How many rows will result contain?
questions.answer: 7 calendar days, although the source has only 6 observations.

questions.prompt: Why not fill the missing day with zero automatically?
questions.answer: No record does not prove that nobody visited; the value is unknown.

cells.task: Build the daily Series and select only entries whose visitor count is missing. Store that filtered Series, retaining its date index, in result and print it.
cells.hint: Filter the daily Series with its isna() mask.
cells.solution:
df = attendance()
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
daily = df.set_index("Date")["Visitors"].sort_index().asfreq("D")
result = daily[daily.isna()]
print(result)
cells.solution_note: Only 2026-10-04 is missing between the observed start and end dates.

options: The true counts for missing days
check.feedback: It creates the requested date grid; it cannot reconstruct unknown measurements.

cells.watch: asfreq does not aggregate. Ensure the date index is unique before requesting a frequency.
cells.takeaway: A gap in records is not automatically a zero.

cells.title: Resample into calendar bins
cells.explanation: resample groups observations into time bins. Here each bin starts at a three-day boundary measured from the first day. Report the number of observations beside the total so a partial bin is visible.
cells.code:
df = attendance()
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
s = df.set_index("Date")["Visitors"].sort_index()
groups = s.resample("3D")
result = pd.DataFrame({"Recorded_Total": groups.sum(min_count=1), "Observed_Days": groups.count()})
print(result)

questions.answer: Observations falling in successive three-day calendar bins.

questions.prompt: What total is recorded for October 1 through October 3?
Is the total of 58 for the next bin a complete three-day total?
questions.answer: No. October 4 is missing, so it includes only the recorded counts for October 5 and 6.

cells.task: Resample to individual days and use sum(min_count=1) so October 4 stays missing. Store only the daily total Series, indexed by date, in result.
cells.hint: Change "3D" to "D" and require at least one known value for a sum.
cells.solution:
df = attendance()
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
s = df.set_index("Date")["Visitors"].sort_index()
result = s.resample("D").sum(min_count=1)
print(result)
cells.solution_note: min_count=1 keeps a day with no observations unknown instead of reporting an empty sum as zero.

check.feedback: A total based on two observed days should not be interpreted as a complete three-day total.

cells.solution_verify:
assert len(result) == 7
assert pd.isna(result.loc["2026-10-04"])
assert result.loc["2026-10-05"] == 30
cells.watch: Time-bin labels and boundaries depend on frequency and options; state the reporting period.
cells.takeaway: Time summaries need a coverage check.

cells.title: Calculate a rolling mean
cells.explanation: A rolling window calculates a statistic repeatedly as it moves through the data. On this daily grid, rolling(3) means three calendar rows. min_periods=3 requires three known counts, so windows crossing the missing day stay unknown.
cells.code:
df = attendance()
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
daily = df.set_index("Date")["Visitors"].sort_index().asfreq("D")
result = pd.DataFrame({"Visitors": daily, "Mean_3_Days": daily.rolling(3, min_periods=3).mean()})
print(result.round(2))

questions.answer: At least three non-missing observations within the current window.

questions.prompt: What is the rolling mean on October 7?
Would rolling(3) mean three days on the original irregular index?
questions.answer: No. It would mean three observed rows, which can span more than three days.

cells.task: Calculate a two-day rolling mean requiring two known daily counts. Store only the resulting mean Series, indexed by date, in result.
cells.hint: Apply rolling(2, min_periods=2).mean() to the daily Series and save that Series directly.
cells.solution:
df = attendance()
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
daily = df.set_index("Date")["Visitors"].sort_index().asfreq("D")
result = daily.rolling(2, min_periods=2).mean()
print(result.round(2))
cells.solution_note: The last two-day mean is also 30, using only October 6 and 7. Earlier windows differ.

check.prompt: Without a regular daily grid, rolling(3) means what?
check.feedback: An integer window size counts rows, regardless of the spacing between timestamps.

cells.solution_verify:
assert result.loc["2026-10-02"] == 22
assert result.loc["2026-10-07"] == 30
assert pd.isna(result.loc["2026-10-05"])
cells.watch: Sort time data before rolling. Otherwise the window follows an unintended order.
cells.takeaway: Window size and missing-data rules both affect a moving average.

cells.title: Compare with a previous period
cells.explanation: shift(1) places the previous row value beside the current row. pct_change(fill_method=None) calculates fractional change without filling gaps. Multiplying by 100 expresses that change as a percentage.
cells.code:
df = attendance()
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
daily = df.set_index("Date")["Visitors"].sort_index().asfreq("D")
result = pd.DataFrame({"Visitors": daily, "Previous_Day": daily.shift(1), "Change_Percent": daily.pct_change(fill_method=None) * 100})
print(result.round(2))

questions.prompt: Why is the first change missing?
questions.answer: There is no previous value in this series for comparison.

questions.prompt: What percentage change is shown on October 2?
Why is the October 5 change unknown?
questions.answer: The previous calendar day, October 4, has no known visitor count.

cells.task: Calculate the signed difference in visitor counts from two calendar days earlier using shift(2). Store the difference Series, indexed by date, in result.
cells.hint: Subtract the shifted daily Series from the original daily Series.
cells.solution:
df = attendance()
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"], format="%Y-%m-%d")
daily = df.set_index("Date")["Visitors"].sort_index().asfreq("D")
result = daily - daily.shift(2)
print(result)
cells.solution_note: October 7 is two visitors higher than October 5. Comparisons involving missing dates stay unknown.

check.feedback: A fractional change of 0.20 corresponds to 20%.

cells.watch: Percent change from a previous zero is undefined; inspect zero denominators.
cells.takeaway: Be explicit about the time interval and denominator.
